title: Operators in depth
summary: The order Excel calculates in, comparisons that answer TRUE or FALSE, joining with &, ranges, and the @ sign.
objectives: Predict a formula’s answer using Excel’s order of operations.
Compare values with =, <>, <, >, <= and >=, and read TRUE or FALSE.
Read the range operator (:), spilled answers and the @ sign in a formula.

p: Excel doesn’t simply work left to right. It follows an order, like BODMAS from school, with two surprises.
Same level? Left to right: =10/2*5 is 25.
When in doubt, add brackets: they cost nothing and show what you mean.
Want −4? Write =-(2^2).
In real life: typed =A2*1+B2/12 instead of =A2*(1+B2/12) and quoted the wrong amount. A pair of brackets fixed it.

p: A comparison asks Excel a yes-or-no question. The answer is **TRUE** or **FALSE**.
The six: `=` equal, `<>` not equal, `<` `>` less or more, `<=` `>=` or equal.
Text comparisons ignore capitals: ="pune"="PUNE" is TRUE.
Comparisons are the tests inside IF, COUNTIF and FILTER, coming up next.
In real life: marks pass or fail with =B2>=33 in one column, then counts the TRUEs for the board report.

why.2: Comparing text with text is fine.
why.3: A comparison always gives TRUE or FALSE.

p: The **&** operator glues values together into one piece of text.
Text you type goes in "double quotes"; a space is " ".
Numbers lose their format when joined: 1250000 joins as 1250000, not ₹12,50,000. Lesson 3.4 fixes that with TEXT.
Dates join as their serial number, like 46203, for the same reason.
In real life: builds address labels with =B2&", "&C2&" - "&D2, which gives “Karol Bagh, New Delhi - 110005”.

p: The colon makes a range. In Microsoft 365 a formula on a range can give many answers that **spill** into the cells below, and **@** asks for just one.
`B2:B5` means every cell from B2 to B5.
=B2:B5*1.18 is typed once, in C2, and fills C2:C5. Module 8 is all about this.
Files from older Excel may show =@B2:B5*1.18. The **@** means “just the value on my own row”, the old behaviour.
In real life: opened a 2015 price file in Microsoft 365 and saw @ signs in some formulas. Nothing was broken: @ keeps the old one-answer behaviour.

demo.intro: Mark who passed with a comparison, then build full names with &.

steps.say: Is Asha’s mark 33 or more? A comparison answers TRUE or FALSE.
Fill down: each row asks the same question about its own student.
Join first name, a space and the surname with &.
One more: what does =2+3*4 give? Multiplication first.

demo.outro: Comparisons give TRUE or FALSE, & joins text, and Excel’s order of operations decides what happens first.

lab.intro: Two quick formulas, then six predictions. For each prediction, work it out in your head first; you can test it in an empty cell of the grid afterwards.

tasks.prompt: In **D2:D6**, show TRUE if the student has 33 marks or more, FALSE if not.
hints: A comparison gives TRUE or FALSE by itself.

tasks.prompt: In **E2:E6**, show each full name: first name, a space, surname.

hints: Excel does the minus sign before the power.
tasks.explain: Negation comes before ^ in Excel: (−3)² = 9. Write =-(3^2) for −9.

hints: Which comes first in a dictionary?
tasks.explain: Alphabetically, apple comes before banana, so it is “less”: TRUE.
Excel does (2³)² = 8² = 64. Maths books would say 2⁹ = 512: use brackets to be sure.

quiz.explain: * happens before &, so 10 is joined on.
7 is equal to 7, so “not equal” is FALSE.

quiz.q: A formula from an old file reads =@B2:B9*2. What does the @ do?
options: It asks for just the value on the formula’s own row
It turns the result into text
quiz.explain: @ is implicit intersection: one value, the way older Excel worked.

points: Excel’s order: brackets, negation, %, ^, × ÷, + −, &, then comparisons. Same level: left to right.
Comparisons (= <> < > <= >=) give **TRUE** or **FALSE**; text ignores capitals.
**&** joins text; **:** makes a range; **@** asks for a single value.
recap.cheat: Brackets first; comparisons give TRUE/FALSE; & joins.

cards.back: **4**: Excel applies the minus sign before the power.

cards.front: Join A2 and B2 with a space
In **C2**, show TRUE if B2 is at least 33.
